prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "NEWMONT Corp /DE/" (ticker NEM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NEM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Newmont Corporation
result.industry: Gold mining (with copper, silver and zinc by-products)
markets: Gold mining and sale of gold dore and concentrate
Silver, zinc and lead by-products (mainly Peñasquito, Mexico)

mission.statement: to create value and improve lives through sustainable and responsible mining
mission.source: Newmont 2025 Form 10-K and company press releases ("At Newmont, our purpose is to create value and improve lives through sustainable and responsible mining.")
mission.plain: Run mines safely and responsibly so that owners, workers and nearby communities all end up better off.

about.plain: Newmont is the world's biggest gold miner. It digs rock out of huge mines in places like Australia, Papua New Guinea, Ghana, Canada, Mexico, Peru and Nevada, crushes it, and pulls out the gold. It also gets copper, silver and zinc from the same rock. In 2025 it produced about 5.9 million ounces of gold and sold $22.7 billion of metals.
about.customers: Refiners, bullion banks and smelters buy its gold, copper and other metals at world market prices.
about.everyday: Gold in jewellery, coins, bank vaults and the tiny contacts inside phones, and copper in wiring, may come from mines like Newmont's Lihir, Cadia or Boddington.

money.plain: Gold from mines such as Lihir, Cadia, Boddington, Tanami, Ahafo and Nevada Gold Mines ($19,304M of 2025 sales)
Copper in concentrate from Cadia, Red Chris and Boddington ($1,438M)
Silver mostly from Peñasquito in Mexico ($1,080M)
Cadia panel caves, Red Chris block cave and Wafi-Golpu, aimed at about 150,000 t a year of copper long term

result.summary: Newmont sells a commodity at the world price, so it has no brand or pricing advantage; its edge is scale and the largest reserve base in the industry (118.2Moz of gold and 12.5Mt of copper reserves at end-2025) in long-life mines such as Lihir, Cadia and Boddington. That cornered-resource advantage is real but narrow, because profits still swing with the gold price and its costs (2025 by-product AISC $1,358/oz, 2026 guidance $1,680/oz) are competitive rather than far below peers.

pricingPower.evidence: It is a price taker: 2025 sales rose 21% to $22,669M because the average realised gold price rose to $3,498/oz, while 2023 ended in a $2,494M loss when costs rose; Q2 2026 realised gold fell to $4,414/oz from the H1 average of $4,661/oz and revenue followed.

moats.evidence: Gold bars are identical whoever mined them, so the Newmont name earns no price premium from refiners or bullion banks.
Buyers can purchase gold or copper concentrate from any producer at market prices with no cost to switch.
More buyers of its metal do not make the product more valuable to other buyers.

As the largest producer (about 5.9Moz attributable gold in 2025, roughly 5% of world mine output) it spreads overheads, exploration and technology over many mines, and its 2025 gold by-product AISC of $1,358/oz was below several large peers, but 2026 guidance rises to $1,680/oz.
Remote mega-mines such as Lihir (Papua New Guinea) and Boddington (Western Australia) face no local rival for the ore body, but gold is sold globally so this does not protect prices.
Its model of owning and operating large gold-copper mines is the same as Barrick's, Agnico Eagle's and AngloGold's.
It has rare block- and panel-cave expertise at Cadia and Red Chris (acquired with Newcrest in 2023) and long experience in deep, complex mines, but large peers have comparable engineering skills.

It holds the industry's largest reserves, 118.2Moz of gold and 12.5Mt of copper at end-2025, in long-life assets (Cadia's panel caves extend life toward mid-century and Lihir's nearshore project targets over 5Moz), which competitors cannot replicate.

customers.evidence: Customers are refiners, bullion banks and smelters buying at market prices; loyalty does not drive demand, but its output always finds buyers through LBMA-accredited refiners and long-standing concentrate offtake contracts.

talent.evidence: It employed about 17,500 people plus 26,600 contractors at end-2025 and has been listed on the Dow Jones Sustainability World Index since 2007, but mining is not a sought-after field for top graduates and it does not appear in major best-employer rankings.

product.evidence: Gold is a commodity, so product quality comes down to mine quality: it owns tier-one assets such as Cadia, Lihir, Boddington and its 38.5% of Nevada Gold Mines, but 2026 output is guided down to about 5.3Moz in what management calls a trough year.

competitors.name: Barrick Mining Corporation
competitors.note: Second-largest gold miner and Newmont's partner in Nevada Gold Mines (Barrick 61.5%) and Pueblo Viejo; also big in copper

competitors.name: Agnico Eagle Mines Limited
competitors.note: Senior gold miner (about 3.45Moz in 2025) in Canada, Australia, Finland and Mexico; competes for assets and investor capital

competitors.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc
competitors.note: Large gold miner (about 3.1Moz) in Africa, Australia and the Americas; neighbour in Ghana and Western Australia

competitors.name: Gold Fields Limited
competitors.note: Gold miner in Australia, Ghana, Peru, Chile and Canada; competes in Western Australia and Ghana

competitors.name: Kinross Gold Corporation
competitors.note: Gold miner in the Americas and West Africa, including Nevada

competitors.name: Zijin Mining Group
competitors.note: Chinese gold and copper giant buying mines worldwide; competes for assets and acquisitions

competitors.name: Northern Star Resources
competitors.note: Large Australian gold producer competing in Western Australia and for Australian mining talent

competitors.name: Freeport-McMoRan
competitors.note: Copper-gold miner (Grasberg) competing in copper and for investor capital

competitors.name: Evolution Mining
competitors.note: Australian gold-copper miner; bought Newcrest's Ernest Henry and Northparkes interests and competes in New South Wales

competitors.name: Harmony Gold Mining Company
competitors.note: South African gold miner and partner of Newmont in the Wafi-Golpu copper-gold project in Papua New Guinea

competitors.name: Endeavour Mining plc
competitors.note: Largest West African gold producer, competing in the region around Ghana

competitors.name: Polyus
competitors.note: Russia's largest gold miner with large reserves; competes only in the global gold market

marketShare.market: Global gold mine production (company 2025 production / World Gold Council 2025 mine production of 3,671.6 t, about 118.0Moz; peer figures approximate)

threats: A fall in the gold price from record levels would cut revenue and margins directly, since it cannot set prices
Rising costs: gold by-product AISC guided to $1,680/oz for 2026 versus $1,358/oz in 2025, with 2026 output dipping to about 5.3Moz

Environmental and legal exposure at Cadia, including a NSW Supreme Court class action filed in February 2026 over tailings dust, PFAS and heavy metals, and a 2025 NSW EPA fine for air-emission offences
Resource nationalism, tax and royalty changes in Ghana, Papua New Guinea, Mexico, Peru and Argentina
Execution risk on long-life growth projects (Cadia panel caves, Lihir nearshore barrier, Tanami Expansion 2, Red Chris block cave)
Reserve depletion: it must keep replacing about 6Moz mined each year
Chinese miners such as Zijin outbidding it for new deposits

ceo.name: Natascha Viljoen
ceo.background: South African metallurgical engineer (BEng, North-West University; Executive MBA, University of Cape Town); former CEO of Anglo American Platinum (2020-2023), earlier roles at Lonmin and BHP; Newmont COO from 2023

c1.evidence: Gold mining is a mature, centuries-old industry; Newmont leads it by size (about 5.9Moz in 2025) but the industry is not emerging, and world mine output grew only fractionally to 3,672t in 2025.

c2.evidence: Buyers choose on price alone, not on brand; what Newmont has that lasts is its 118.2Moz gold and 12.5Mt copper reserve base, which is hard to copy but does not make customers prefer its metal.

c3.evidence: Newmont is the largest gold miner and well known to investors, but few ordinary people recognise the name and customers buy gold, not a Newmont product.

c4.evidence: Its stated purpose is "to create value and improve lives through sustainable and responsible mining" and it stresses safety and sustainability, but the mission is generic for the sector and management is judged mainly on cash flow and returns.

c6.evidence: “biggest gold miner, gold-price play, mining giant”: the impression is mostly neutral to positive among investors, with criticism focused on environmental issues such as Cadia's tailings dust.

c7.evidence: The gold market is huge (record total demand of 5,002t in 2025 per the World Gold Council) and helped by central-bank buying, but physical mine supply grows slowly and Newmont's output is guided down to 5.3Moz in 2026.

c8.evidence: It can grow in copper (long-term goal of about 150,000t a year from Cadia, Red Chris and Wafi-Golpu), but it remains a metals miner with no route into unrelated big markets.

m1.evidence: Natascha Viljoen has a clear operational plan (about 6Moz gold and 150,000t copper long term, focus on a core portfolio of tier-one assets) but not a transformative vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Viljoen is a professional manager who became CEO on January 1, 2026 after joining as COO in 2023, not a founder.

m4.evidence: She emphasises safety and has spoken about mining's legacy and inclusion at her October 2026 Joburg Indaba Hall of Fame induction, but there is no clear evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Newmont's culture centres on safety, cost and capital discipline rather than inventing new products or technologies.

m6.evidence: Viljoen is a metallurgical engineer with more than 30 years of hands-on mining operations experience, including running Anglo American Platinum and serving as Newmont's COO.

m7.evidence: She has spoken publicly about mining's responsibilities to communities and was inducted into the Joburg Indaba Mining Hall of Fame in 2026; there is no record of controversy, but no evidence of stewardship aimed at humanity's benefit beyond the sector norm.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Natascha Viljoen giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: She is a low-profile, operations-focused executive rather than a famous public personality.

m9.evidence: As COO she oversaw delivery of the Newcrest integration and record 2025 free cash flow of $7.3B; as CEO since January 2026 H1 2026 free cash flow was $5,349M, but her CEO record is less than a year old.

m10.evidence: Newmont cut G&A from $442M in 2024 to $382M in 2025 and to $153M in H1 2026 versus $205M a year earlier, but it is not famous for frugality.

c10.evidence: Gold is mainly a store of value and jewellery material; its products do not greatly improve the lives of very large numbers of people the way Netflix or Google do, although its copper helps electrification.

p2.evidence: Building and running mines like the Cadia panel caves or Lihir in Papua New Guinea is very hard, and copper is important to electrification, but gold itself is not critical to the world's progress.

f2.evidence: Gross margin after mining costs and depreciation rose from 36.4% in 2020 to 53.2% in 2025 and operating margin from 24.4% to 48.4%, but both collapsed in between (operating margin was negative in 2023).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 cash of $9,009M exceeded debt of $5,083M, trailing operating cash flow was $12.6B and stockholders' equity was $35,243M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $2,806M in 2020 to $10,961M in 2025 and operating cash flow from $4,890M to $10,334M, but both fell sharply in 2022-2023.

v1.evidence: Gold is identical whoever mines it, so there is no reason for a buyer to pick Newmont's gold over anyone else's.

v2.evidence: Newmont is not on major best-employer lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For; its recognitions are ESG ones like the Dow Jones Sustainability World Index (since 2007).

c5.evidence: If Newmont vanished, its roughly 17,500 employees, host communities and governments in places like Ghana, Papua New Guinea and Nevada would miss it, but other miners would supply the gold and the world's gold price would barely change.
